tagline: A damaged genetic manuscript has lost its orientation and pairing marks. Rebuild it from nucleotide parts and restore the information stored in its sequence.

guide.name: Nia Sol
guide.visual: black archivist coat, gold page clips, violet inspection lamp
guide.story_job: keeps one damaged nucleic-acid manuscript with you while each room restores a different structural feature

premise: A humidity-control failure has torn apart one of the archive’s genetic manuscripts. Bases, sugars, phosphates, strand directions, and pairing marks are scattered across ten rooms.
mission: Reconstruct the manuscript with Nia. Distinguish DNA from RNA, nucleotide from nucleoside, purines from pyrimidines, 5′ from 3′ ends, strand direction, antiparallel geometry, base pairing, and what happens when DNA melts apart.
finale: At the DNA Melting Room, the restored manuscript separates cleanly into two intact strands and then re-pairs. Nia shelves it again, and the route behind you reads like one structural sentence: units connect directionally, sequence stores information, and complementary antiparallel strands create the DNA double helix.
learner_rule: Read or listen and picture the scene. The important terms are introduced inside the action. Stop only when a Quick Recall appears.
route_orientation: The archive is a long reading hall wrapped around a central spiral staircase. You begin at the front desk, move through component rooms and the backbone bridge, climb the antiparallel stair, inspect base pairing, and finish in the controlled melting chamber.

scenes.story_open: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **DNA/RNA Front Desk**. The archive entrance contains two damaged manuscript cases. A heavy double-scroll case labeled DNA sits left. A lighter single-scroll case labeled RNA sits right. A central information vault waits for both. The DNA case is on your left, the Information vault is directly ahead, and the RNA case marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.
story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **DNA/RNA Front Desk**. The archive entrance contains two damaged manuscript cases. A heavy double-scroll case labeled DNA sits left. A lighter single-scroll case labeled RNA sits right. A central information vault waits for both. The DNA case is on your left, the Information vault is directly ahead, and the RNA case marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.
Nia Sol opens the two cases. Both manuscripts belong to the same molecular family: **nucleic acids**, polymers of nucleotides involved in storing, transmitting, and expressing hereditary information.

The left case is **DNA**, deoxyribonucleic acid. The right is **RNA**, ribonucleic acid. They share a nucleotide-based architecture but differ in sugar, one nitrogenous base, and their usual strand organization.

Nia places the two manuscript types side by side and names them together: **DNA and RNA**. DNA is deoxyribonucleic acid; RNA is ribonucleic acid. The rest of the archive will show why their structural differences matter.
A torn strip from the DNA case slides across the desk. Nia places it under the first inspection lamp. “Before we rebuild a strand, we need to know exactly what one unit contains.”
scenes.story_close: A torn strip from the DNA case slides across the desk. Nia places it under the first inspection lamp. “Before we rebuild a strand, we need to know exactly what one unit contains.”

scenes.story_open: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **Nucleotide Pass Counter**. A customs-style counter has three trays labeled BASE, SUGAR, and PHOSPHATE. A page receives a gold pass only when all three pieces are present. A side lane removes the phosphate and prints a different label. The Nitrogenous-base tray is on your left, the Nucleotide assembly is directly ahead, and the Nucleoside lane marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.
story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **Nucleotide Pass Counter**. A customs-style counter has three trays labeled BASE, SUGAR, and PHOSPHATE. A page receives a gold pass only when all three pieces are present. A side lane removes the phosphate and prints a different label. The Nitrogenous-base tray is on your left, the Nucleotide assembly is directly ahead, and the Nucleoside lane marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.

Nia places a nitrogenous base in the first tray, a five-carbon sugar in the second, and a phosphate in the third. Together those components form a **nucleotide**. Free nucleotide precursors can carry additional phosphates during cellular reactions, but the nucleotide incorporated into a strand contributes one phosphate to the repeating backbone.

She removes the phosphate from a second model. Base plus sugar without phosphate is a **nucleoside**. The words sound similar because the structures are similar; the phosphate is the decisive difference.

On the finished strand model, phosphate groups sit between neighboring sugars as part of the sugar-phosphate backbone. The pass counter releases the base pieces into a reading room where their ring shapes are projected onto the walls.

story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **DNA/RNA Sugar Gallery**. Two long display cases run parallel down the gallery. The DNA case contains deoxyribose sugar and thymine cards. The RNA case contains ribose sugar and uracil cards. Adenine, cytosine, and guanine appear in both. Nia places the DNA and RNA sugar cards beside each other. DNA contains **deoxyribose**; RNA contains **ribose**. The names of the nucleic acids preserve that distinction.
She then slides a T card into the DNA case: **thymine** is used in DNA. In the RNA case, a U card takes its place: **uracil** is used in RNA. Adenine, cytosine, and guanine remain available to both.
The two cases now have enough identity to rebuild a strand. Their component trays move onto a narrow bridge where the 5′ and 3′ ends are marked in gold.

scenes.story_open: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **Backbone Bridge**. A narrow bridge is built from alternating sugar tiles and phosphate rails. A large 5′ marker stands at the entrance beside a phosphate. A 3′ marker stands at the far end beside a free hydroxyl group. story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **Backbone Bridge**. A narrow bridge is built from alternating sugar tiles and phosphate rails. A large 5′ marker stands at the entrance beside a phosphate. A 3′ marker stands at the far end beside a free hydroxyl group. The 5′ end is on your left, the Sugar-phosphate backbone is directly ahead, and the 3′ end marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.
At the bridge entrance, Nia taps the **5′ phosphate end**. The 5′ label refers to carbon numbering in the sugar, and the strand end here is associated with phosphate at the 5′ carbon.
Across the bridge, alternating sugar and phosphate groups create the backbone. Neighboring nucleotide units are covalently connected through **phosphodiester linkages**.

At the far rail, the strand terminates with a free **3′ hydroxyl end**. These two different ends give the strand directionality. Nia clips a new nucleotide to her belt and leads you to the growth desk built beside the 3′ end.

scenes.story_open: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **3′ Growth Desk**. A drafting desk is attached directly to the 3′ end of the backbone bridge. New nucleotide cards approach on a feeder rail and can connect only at the free 3′ hydroxyl end. The Older 5′ region is on your left, the Growing strand is directly ahead, and the 3′ addition desk marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.
story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **3′ Growth Desk**. A drafting desk is attached directly to the 3′ end of the backbone bridge. New nucleotide cards approach on a feeder rail and can connect only at the free 3′ hydroxyl end. The Older 5′ region is on your left, the Growing strand is directly ahead, and the 3′ addition desk marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.

Nia tries the new nucleotide at the 5′ end. The tool refuses it. She moves to the free 3′ hydroxyl and the nucleotide locks into place. During nucleic-acid synthesis, **new nucleotides are added to the 3′ end** of the growing strand.

Because growth occurs at that end, the strand is synthesized in the **5′→3′ direction**. The 5′ and 3′ labels are therefore not decorative arrows; they describe real chemical directionality in the backbone.
The one-way tool demonstrates **nucleotide addition to 3′ end**: each incoming nucleotide is attached at the growing strand's free 3′ end, so synthesis proceeds in the 5′→3′ direction.
Each new addition lengthens the manuscript by one base. The growing strip feeds into a cataloging machine that reads the bases not merely as parts, but as information.
scenes.story_close: Each new addition lengthens the manuscript by one base. The growing strip feeds into a cataloging machine that reads the bases not merely as parts, but as information.

The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.

Nia holds two strips with the same length and the same collection of base cards. Their orders differ, so their information differs. Biological information is encoded in the **linear nucleotide sequence**, not simply in the number of nucleotides present.
In a gene, that sequence ultimately specifies an amino-acid sequence, connecting nucleic-acid information to protein structure and function.

The restored DNA sequence is ready, but its second strand is lying upside down beside it. Nia carries both strips toward the central spiral staircase, where opposite direction is built into the architecture.

story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **Antiparallel Spiral Staircase**. Two rails wind around a central spiral staircase. One rail begins 5′ at the bottom and reaches 3′ at the top. The neighboring rail begins 3′ at the bottom and reaches 5′ at the top. The Strand A is on your left, the Double-helix axis is directly ahead, and the Strand B marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.
Nia lays one DNA strand along the left rail. Its 5′ end begins low and its 3′ end rises. The second strand can pair properly only when its direction is reversed: 3′ at the bottom and 5′ at the top.
That opposite orientation is **antiparallel**. DNA consists of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands twisted into a **double helix**.
As the rails twist upward, base cards turn inward toward one another. The staircase opens onto a reading table where the pairing rules are built into matching slots.

story_paragraphs: Nia Sol carries the damaged genetic manuscript into **Base-Pair Reading Table**. A long reading table has matching base slots. A fits only T in the DNA tray; C fits G. Beside it, an RNA ribbon folds back on itself so A pairs with U and C pairs with G. The A–T tray is on your left, the C–G tray is directly ahead, and the RNA fold marks the other side of the archive. The same strip of nucleic acid remains in your hands, so each repair changes one identifiable part of the manuscript.

On the DNA side, **adenine pairs with thymine** through hydrogen bonds. **Cytosine pairs with guanine** through hydrogen bonds. These complementary relationships place a purine opposite a pyrimidine inside the double helix.

The RNA ribbon behaves differently as a whole: RNA is **typically single stranded**, yet complementary regions of one RNA molecule can fold back and pair with each other. In RNA, **adenine pairs with uracil**, while **cytosine can pair with guanine** just as C–G pairing occurs in DNA.
Nia places the fully paired DNA manuscript into a temperature-controlled chamber. The final test will separate the strands without cutting the covalent backbones.

scenes.title: Separate the Strands Without Cutting Them
scenes.scene_kicker: Heating can disrupt noncovalent pairing while leaving each covalent backbone intact.
scenes.location_description: A temperature chamber holds three paired DNA strips. One is rich in A–T pairs, one in G–C pairs, and one mixed. Dotted hydrogen bonds disappear as temperature rises, but the sugar-phosphate rails remain unbroken.

zones.label: Melting chamber
zones.description: Heat disrupts the noncovalent interactions stabilizing the double helix and separates the strands.

zones.label: G–C-rich sample
zones.description: Each G–C pair contributes three hydrogen bonds and higher GC content generally raises melting temperature under comparable conditions.

scenes.story_open: The first cards make the pairwise difference clear: an **A–T base pair forms two hydrogen bonds**, while a **G–C base pair forms three**. That contributes to stability, but Nia immediately covers a sign that says THREE IS THE ONLY REASON. DNA duplex stability also depends on sequence-dependent stacking, strand length, ionic conditions, and other thermodynamic effects.
story_paragraphs: The first cards make the pairwise difference clear: an **A–T base pair forms two hydrogen bonds**, while a **G–C base pair forms three**. That contributes to stability, but Nia immediately covers a sign that says THREE IS THE ONLY REASON. DNA duplex stability also depends on sequence-dependent stacking, strand length, ionic conditions, and other thermodynamic effects.

She raises the temperature. The dotted interactions between complementary bases disappear and the two strands separate. This is **DNA denaturation**. The covalent sugar-phosphate backbones remain intact during ordinary thermal denaturation; the manuscript has opened, not been chopped into nucleotides.

Under comparable conditions, DNA regions with higher **GC content** generally melt at higher temperatures than equivalent lower-GC regions. The bond-count difference contributes, but it is not a complete mechanistic explanation by itself.

Nia calls the side-by-side cards a **base-pair hydrogen-bond count comparison**. A–T forms two hydrogen bonds and G–C forms three, although that count is only one contributor to overall DNA duplex stability.

Nia cools the chamber and the complementary strands pair again. She clips the restored manuscript into its case. From base + sugar + phosphate to directional backbone, sequence, antiparallel helix, complementary pairing, and melting, the archive is readable again.
